blocks.text: API architecture covers how an LLM API service is actually structured, distinct endpoints for different capabilities, a stateless request cycle, synchronous versus streaming response patterns, and critically, where that API call should actually sit within your own application design.

This topic covers different endpoints for different capabilities, why LLM APIs are typically stateless, the difference between synchronous and streaming response patterns, and the important architectural point that an API key should never be exposed directly in client side code.
1. What API Architecture Means Here

blocks.alt: Building on what an LLM API is, API architecture covers how the service is structured

blocks.text: API architecture covers the structural patterns behind how an LLM API is actually organized, its endpoints, its request lifecycle, and how it typically fits within a broader application, rather than the specific request and response format details, covered in the next module.
2. Different Endpoints for Different Capabilities

blocks.alt: A chat completions endpoint, an embeddings endpoint, and a models list endpoint each serve different purposes

blocks.text: A typical LLM API exposes several distinct endpoints, a chat or completions endpoint for generating text, an embeddings endpoint, covered in a later module, for generating vector representations, and often a models endpoint for listing available models, each endpoint has its own specific request shape suited to its purpose.
3. Stateless Request-Response Design

blocks.alt: Each request is independent, with no server side memory of past requests

blocks.text: This connects directly to the memory instructions concept covered in an earlier module, most LLM APIs are stateless, each request stands entirely on its own, the provider does not remember a previous call, an application needing conversation history has to explicitly resend that entire history with every single request.

code.content:
# Stateless: full conversation history sent with every call
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "The capital of France is Paris."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is its population?"},
]

blocks.text: 4. Synchronous vs Streaming Response Patterns

blocks.alt: A synchronous pattern waits for the full response, a streaming pattern receives tokens as they are generated

blocks.text: A synchronous call waits until the model has finished generating the entire response before returning anything, a streaming call, covered in full depth in a later topic in this module, returns generated tokens incrementally as they are produced, letting an application display a response progressively rather than waiting for it to complete entirely.

blocks.text: 5. Where the API Call Fits in Your Application

blocks.alt: A client sends a request to your own backend server, which calls the provider LLM API

blocks.text: A well architected application routes API calls through its own backend server, rather than calling the provider API directly from a client application, the client talks to your backend, your backend talks to the provider API, this pattern is standard for any external API integration, not unique to LLM APIs specifically.
6. API Versioning

blocks.alt: API version 1 evolves into API version 2

blocks.text: Provider APIs evolve over time, and most include an explicit version identifier in their request structure, allowing a provider to introduce changes or new capabilities in a new version while existing applications built against an older version continue working unaffected until they choose to migrate.
7. Never Exposing an API Key in Client Side Code

blocks.alt: Exposing an API key directly in browser code is a genuine security risk

blocks.text: This connects directly to the input validation and security concerns covered in an earlier module, an API key embedded directly in client side browser or mobile app code is visible to anyone who inspects that code, exposing your credentials and potentially your entire API budget to abuse, this is exactly why the backend routing pattern covered above matters, the API key stays server side, never reaching the client.

blocks.title: This is one of the most common and consequential architectural mistakes
blocks.content: A leaked API key embedded in public client side code can be discovered and abused within hours of a mistaken deployment, this specific architectural discipline, never exposing credentials client side, deserves particular attention.

blocks.text: 8. A Worked Architecture Example

A well structured chat application has its frontend send a user message to its own backend server, the backend attaches the API key, assembles the full conversation history since the API is stateless, calls the provider API, and returns only the response content back to the frontend, the API key itself never travels to or through the client.
9. API Architecture and the Rest of This Module

This topic sets up the remaining topics in this module directly, authentication and API keys cover the credential side of this architecture in depth, rate limiting and quotas cover usage constraints, and streaming APIs and WebSockets go deeper into the response pattern options introduced here.
Worked Example

A team initially prototypes a feature by calling a provider API directly from their web frontend for speed, quickly realizing during a security review that this exposes their API key to anyone viewing their site source code.

Restructuring the application to route all API calls through their own backend server, with the key stored only server side, resolves this exposure entirely, while also giving them a natural place to add the rate limiting and monitoring practices covered later in this course.
Common Mistakes

items: Calling a provider API directly from client side code, exposing the API key to anyone inspecting that code
Assuming an LLM API remembers previous requests rather than resending full conversation history each time
Not considering whether a synchronous or streaming response pattern actually fits the application user experience
Ignoring API versioning and building against behavior that could change in a future provider update

blocks.text: Practice

Sketch out the architecture for an application that needs to call an LLM API, specifically identifying where the API key would be stored, and confirm your design never requires that key to travel to or be visible in client side code.
Key Takeaway

LLM API architecture involves distinct endpoints for different capabilities, a typically stateless request cycle requiring full context resent each call, a choice between synchronous and streaming response patterns, and critically, routing calls through your own backend server so an API key never reaches client side code where it could be exposed.
